The user's question is about whether individuals who have undergone a cerebral hemispherectomy (removal of one side of the brain) and have retained some reading abilities can still read, specifically focusing on the right hemisphere. 

To address this, we need to consider what happens during a cerebral hemispherectomy and how it affects language processing in both hemispheres.

A cerebral hemispherectomy is performed to alleviate severe epilepsy symptoms by removing the seizure focus from one side of the brain. This can involve damaging or removing various parts of the left hemisphere (which processes language) as well, leading to potential language deficits on that side.

The question remains whether individuals who have undergone such a procedure and still retain some reading abilities indicate that their isolated right hemisphere is capable of supporting literacy. 

Research has shown that even after hemispherectomy, remnants of language processing can remain in certain areas of the brain, including the left hemisphere's posterior parietal cortex and Broca's area (the right hemisphere). However, these areas may not be as strongly connected to reading or writing tasks as those on the left side.

Despite this, some studies suggest that individuals with residual left-hemisphere language capabilities can still engage in reading activities and develop literacy skills. However, the extent of this capability varies widely among individuals post-hemispherectomy.

Given these considerations, it appears that retained reading abilities are unlikely solely due to damage to the isolated right hemisphere after cerebral hemispherectomy. Instead, they may be related to residual language processing capabilities in the left hemisphere or other areas of the brain involved in language and literacy.

In summary, while the retained reading abilities might not exclusively result from damage to the isolated right hemisphere post-hemispherectomy, the complexity of human cognition and the variability among individuals with such procedures suggest that this capability cannot be solely attributed to residual right-hemisphere function.
